newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland TV debate fails to answer key questions.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland TV debate fails to answer key questions.

text.p: Hopes for peace in Northern Ireland drew scant encouragement on Tuesday from an unprecedented televised debate between key pro-Irish and pro-British foes who are supposed to negotiate a lasting settlement in September.

Newspaper commentators said the half-hour showdown between Ken Maginnis of the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) and Martin McGuinness of Sinn Fein was either a narrow win for Sinn Fein or a moral triumph for the UUP.
It also failed to shed any light on whether the UUP will actually sit down and negotiate with its Sinn Fein rivals when Anglo-Irish peace talks resume in earnest in September.
"Grumpy Ken loses out to muddled Martin" was the headline in the Irish News, a newspaper generally read by the Catholic minority from which Sinn Fein, political wing of IRA guerrillas, draws support.
"And of course, not one word either said changed anyone's mind in the north," the newspaper said.

Commentators said that although the debate was without precedent in Britain, it merely rehearsed age-old arguments at the heart of the conflict over which the two sides have failed to agree for almost three decades.
The Belfast Newsletter, read mainly by Protestant unionists who want Northern Ireland to stay British, trumpeted Maginnis's longstanding allegation that McGuinness is an IRA leader on its front page.
"Accused" read the headline of its Wednesday edition above a story which said unionists had "exposed Sinn Fein's reluctance to accept a democratic agenda at next month's all-party talks."

Maginnis accused McGuinness of being the "Godfather of Godfathers" of the IRA, whose 28-year war against British rule was halted by a July 20 ceasefire which will admit Sinn Fein to the talks if it is deemed genuine.
But Maginnis failed to say whether the UUP will sit at the same table as Sinn Fein to forge a settlement of the 28-year conflict.
"We won't be abdicating our responsibility to society in Northern Ireland," he told the BBC after it staged the first debate between the two in Britain.
"We cannot take seriously an organisation which portrays itself as political Sinn Fein when in fact it is very clearly military IRA," he said.

He even refused to shake hands with his rival after the 27-minute debate, which was watched by an estimated one million people, two thirds of Northern Ireland's 60 per cent Protestant and 40 percent Catholic population.

McGuinness calmly denied allegations of being an IRA leader, as he has for years, acknowledged that he was twice convicted of IRA membership in Ireland in the 1970s and sidestepped key questions about the talks.
He refused to publicly accept the view of Britain and Ireland that the people of Northern Ireland should determine the province's status.
Sinn Fein wants any vote to include the Irish republic, whose constitution claims Northern Ireland and its people.
He also refused to budge from Sinn Fein's long-held position that the surrender or decommissioning of IRA arms should be negotiated as part of a final settlement, rather than during the talks.
Maginnis said the July 20 IRA truce was a ploy and said the guerrillas would go back to war if a settlement fell short of the united Ireland they seek.
McGuinness said he was encouraged by the fact that Maginnis had accepted the debate invitation. Maginnis appeared once before on a U.S. televised debate with Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams.
"I am very encouraged by the fact that Ken Maginnis and other unionists accept that the people I represent need to be involved in the discussions," he said.
Both McGuinness and Adams won seats in the British parliament in May 1 elections but have refused to take the oath of allegiance to Britain that would allow them to occupy their seats.
McGuinness announced before the debate that he would be appealing against the British parliament's decision to refuse the two Sinn Fein MPs the right to sit in the assembly without taking the oath.
